Title: Intelligent automated code review and software quality evaluation: a survey of AutoML and large language model techniques
Abstract: Automated code review and software quality evaluation have become central concerns in modern software engineering, where rapid development cycles and large, continuously evolving codebases strain traditional manual quality assurance. This survey synthesises research from 2020 to 2026 on AI-driven techniques for code review and software quality evaluation, focusing on two complementary paradigms: Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) and Large Language Models (LLMs). AutoML methods-including neural architecture search (NAS), hyperparameter optimisation (HPO), and meta-learning-automatically construct and optimise predictive models for defect prediction, bug localisation, and code smell detection, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering and expert configuration. Foundation models and LLMs pre-trained on large code corpora-CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5, Codex, Code Llama, and instruction-tuned conversational agents such as ChatGPT and GPT-4-have demonstrated strong capabilities in code understanding, generation, and review assistance, enabling automated review-comment generation, vulnerability detection, and refactoring suggestions, while still requiring careful calibration and human verification for deployment-critical use. We organise the literature along a task taxonomy encompassing defect and vulnerability prediction, code smell and maintainability assessment, review-comment generation, and DevOps analytics, and systematically compare AutoML-driven and LLM-driven techniques across effectiveness, scalability, and interpretability. Multi-modal learning and human-AI collaboration are highlighted as emerging dimensions of state-of-the-art systems. Empirical benchmarks including Defects4J, Big-Vul, CodeXGLUE, SWE-bench, and NPRComment are reviewed to characterise evaluation practices and reproducibility norms. Critical open challenges-scaling to real-time CI/CD, cross-project generalisation, developer-legible explanations, and trust calibration-are identified, and a structured six-point research agenda is outlined.

Title: Large Language Models for Fault Localization: An Empirical Study
Source: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOFTWARE ENGINEERING AND KNOWLEDGE ENGINEERING
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on code-related tasks, particularly in automated program repair. However, repair effectiveness often depends on accurate upstream fault localization, while the statement-level fault localization capability of LLMs remains insufficiently evaluated. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of LLMs for statement-level fault localization. We evaluate four representative LLMs, including two open-weight models, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and DeepSeek-V3 and two closed-source models, GPT-4.1 mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, on HumanEval-Java and Defects4J. The evaluation covers different input contexts and prompt strategies, including Zero-shot, Few-shot and Chain-of-Thought prompting. We further assess model performance from three complementary perspectives: Exact Match, Partial Match and output consistency and compare LLMs with representative non-LLM baselines, including PMD and LineDef, under the same source-code-only input setting. In addition, we analyze practical efficiency and cost in terms of end-to-end response time and token-based API cost. The results show that bug report context improves observed fault localization performance on Defects4J. Few-shot prompting improves performance in some cases but does not yield consistent gains and Chain-of-Thought prompting shows mixed effects across models. Overall, this study reveals the strengths, limitations, and practical trade-offs of LLMs in statement-level fault localization, providing empirical evidence for model selection and application in software engineering practice.
